title: Putin cites chance of peace deal, Zelenskiy says US negotiators to visit both countries
description: VLADIVOSTOK, Russia, Sept 3 (Reuters) - Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Thursday there was a chance of reaching an agreement to end the war in Ukraine, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zel...
fullText:
VLADIVOSTOK, Russia, Sept 3 (Reuters) - Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Thursday there was a chance of reaching an agreement to end the war in Ukraine, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said U.S. negotiators trying to broker a deal would ‌soon visit both Moscow and Kyiv.

Putin, speaking at an economic forum in Russia's far east, said a number of countries including the U.S. ‌and China were ready to support a peace settlement.

"Ultimately, however, the problem must be resolved by the countries involved in the conflict — Russia and Ukraine," he said.

"We are grateful to everyone ​attempting to contribute to a settlement. Is there a chance? In my view, yes, there is."

In Kyiv, Zelenskiy said in his nightly video address that preliminary dates had been set for a visit by U.S. negotiators.

"We expect to see representatives of the U.S. president here in Kyiv," Zelenskiy said.

"There will be a meeting with them in Moscow and in Kyiv. We are expecting a meeting with them in the coming days. It is very important. It is important that America ‌continues to be active."

In Washington, U.S. President Donald Trump ⁠said he wanted to see an end to the war and losses sustained by both sides.

"I just want to see that end. I think we'll get it," Trump told GB News in an interview that aired on Thursday, a day ⁠after telling reporters he wanted a summit with Putin when the Kremlin leader is ready for a peace deal.

After 4-1/2 years of Europe's deadliest conflict since World War Two, it is rare for either side to offer an upbeat assessment of peace prospects. They last met for U.S.-mediated talks in February.

Since then, with the U.S. ​distracted by ​the Iran war, both Russia and Ukraine have ramped up long-range air attacks deep ​inside the other's territory. Hostilities at sea have escalated sharply ‌with attacks by both sides on ports and commercial shipping, pushing up global grain prices.

U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who have spearheaded the effort to broker an agreement, were last in Moscow in January. They have yet to visit Kyiv.

Chicago wheat futures dropped by more than 2% on Putin's comments.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha had earlier told reporters in Kyiv that he saw a "new dynamic" coming in peace efforts, with more active political and diplomatic engagement.

Neither side, however, gave reasons to expect progress.

On the contrary, the Kremlin leader said Ukraine's latest actions presented an obstacle.

In response to a question, Putin ‌said Ukrainian attacks on civilian merchant ships and "reported threats of attacks on civilian aircraft" ​were "acts of state terrorism", which he said "complicates the prospects for bilateral peace talks".

Zelenskiy warned airlines ​and insurance companies this week that the presence of Ukrainian drones had ​made Russian skies dangerous, although he said Ukraine would target only Russian military facilities and not threaten civilian aircraft.

On ‌Wednesday, Ukraine urged the U.N.'s aviation agency to ask members to ​ban operations in Russian airspace. Ukraine ​has been cut off from international civil aviation because its own airspace is considered unsafe since Russia invaded in 2022.

PUTIN: CONTACTS MOSTLY TAKE PLACE VIA INTELLIGENCE AGENCIES

Putin said contacts with Ukraine were still taking place.

"It is difficult for me to say right now to what extent these ​contacts are leading to a peace agreement, given ‌the statements we have heard recently from Ukraine's top leadership," he said.

"However, contacts do exist and are continuing on an ongoing basis - ​gain, primarily through intelligence channels."

(Additional reporting by Reuters in Moscow, Max Hunder in Kyiv, Anna Pruchnicka in Gdansk and Tabahriti, Sam ​in London); Writing by Mark Trevelyan; Editing by Andrew Heavens and David Gregorio)

title: Russian general accused of masterminding the attack against Kyiv’s children’s hospital injured in assassination attempt
description: A Russian general who has been accused by Ukraine of ordering a missile strike against a children’s hospital in Kyiv has reportedly been shot in northwestern Russia on Thursday.
fullText:
A Russian general who has been accused by Ukraine of ordering a missile strike against a children's hospital in Kyiv has reportedly been shot in northwestern Russia on Thursday.

The Russian Investigative Committee said it opened an investigation into the attempted murder of a military service member who was shot several times in the city of Engels in the Saratov region on Thursday.

While the committee did not name the man, Russian telegram channels widely reported it was Major General Nikolai Varpakhovich, the commander of the 22nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Division of the Russian Aerospace Forces' Long-Range Aviation.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky later alluded to the attack in his daily address, saying "we will also carry out our own asymmetric operations in response" to Russia.

"The Russian criminals did not hide - they will be found. And today brings another confirmation of this fact, a confirmation in the Saratov region," he added.

Engels serves as the home base of Russia's strategic bombers fleet, including the Tu-95MS and Tu-160 aircraft that Moscow uses to launch long-range cruise missiles against Ukraine.

Varpakhovich has been accused by Ukraine of ordering a missile strike against Kyiv's Okhmatdyt hospital in July 2024.

The attack killed three people – one of them a child who was wounded in the strike and died a few days later – and injured dozens others. Several of the hospital's departments, including the intensive care units, the oncology and surgical wings, the toxicology and trauma center, were damaged or destroyed.

The hospital said afterwards that hundreds of patients and staff were evacuated when the air raid alarm was raised indicating an incoming an strike. But some, including three patients undergoing a heart surgery, were still there when the missile hit about an hour later.

Varpakhovich has also been sanctioned by multiple countries and the European Union over his role in the 2024

While Ukraine has not commented on the incident, Varpakhovych has recently been on Kyiv's radar.

The Security Service of Ukraine and the country's Prosecutor General formally charged him with war crimes three days ago, saying he ordered the long-range aviation units under his command to launch a Kh-101 air-to-ground cruise missile against the hospital.

The Russian investigative committee said the serviceman survived the attack and was transported to a hospital. Local media reported that he was flown to Moscow for treatment after being shot in the face and the torso.

Varpakhovich is the latest of high-profile military officials targeted in apparent assassinations in Russia over the past few years. Moscow has pointed finger at Ukraine over these killings, but Kyiv has never officially acknowledged playing a role in any of them.

Igor Kirillov, a general in charge of the Russian military's nuclear and chemical weapons protection forces, was killed in December 2024 when an explosive device planted on a scooter was detonated near him.

Lt. Gen. Yaroslav Moskalik, deputy head of the main operational department of the General Staff and Lt. Gen. Fanil Sarvarov, who ran the armed forces operational training department, were both killed in car explosions in Moscow last year.

Others who have been killed include the founder of a pro-Russian militia group, Armen Sarkisyan, described by Ukraine as a "criminal mastermind," who died following a bombing in central Moscow, in February 2025.

title: Zelenskyy says foreign airlines suspend Russia flights after Ukrainian warning
description: Zelenskyy said this week that Russian airspace "will effectively be closing."
fullText:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday that the first airlines had begun suspending flights to Russian airports following his vow earlier this week to force the closure of Russian airspace through expanded drone attacks.

"We're getting word that the first airlines have started to suspend flights to Russian airports following our announcement about the drone hazard that objectively exists in Russian airspace," Zelenskyy said in a post to X.

"Ukraine has already officially informed international organizations and our partners about the real situation in Russian airspace," Zelenskyy added.

Disruption to Russian airports and flights have become routine during Moscow's full-scale invasion of its neighbor, as Ukraine has expanded its long-range drone and missile strikes on targets deep into Russian territory.

Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow resume hours after CIA director's visit, mayor says

Ukraine scales up drone attacks in Moscow, across Russia to record highs, data shows

Each night brings temporary restrictions on flights at airports across western and southern Russia, which also often extend to Moscow's international airports.

Ukraine's airspace has been closed since Russia's full-scale invasion began on Feb. 24, 2022. This week, Zelenskyy said that due to "drone infested skies," Russian airspace "will effectively be closing -- the war started by Russia is closing its skies."

On Wednesday night into Thursday morning, Russia's federal air transport agency -- Rosaviatsiya -- announced temporary flight restrictions at airports in Sochi, Gelendzhik, Penza, Saratov, Yaroslavl and Nizhny Novgorod.

All four of Moscow's international airports -- Vnukovo, Sheremetyevo, Domodedovo and Zhukovsky -- were also put under flight restrictions, Rosaviatsiya said in posts to Telegram.

Russia's escalating strikes in Ukraine increasingly spilling into NATO, Romania says

Russia's Defense Ministry said that its forces downed 416 Ukrainian drones overnight into Thursday morning. The craft were shot down over 15 Russian regions, plus occupied Crimea and the Black Sea, the ministry said in a post to Telegram.

At least 116 drones were shot down en route to Moscow, the capital's Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said in posts to Telegram.

Russian authorities have dismissed Zelenskyy's warning. On Wednesday evening, Rosaviatsiya said in a statement that Ukraine's NOTAM -- a Notice to Air Missions, an official warning to air crews of flight hazards -- was "illegitimate."

"All documents published by Ukraine concerning Russian airspace have no legal force and violate the Convention on International Civil Aviation," Rosaviatsiya added. "Russian air transport, its ground infrastructure, continue to operate normally, receiving and dispatching flights, including those of foreign airlines."

'The damage is enormous': Ukraine grapples with record-breaking Russian missile strikes

Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday said Zelenskyy's threat constituted "state‑sponsored terrorism." The Russian leader added that if any related air accidents occur, "We will find something to respond with."

Ukraine has significantly expanded the scale of its drone attacks into Russia in recent months, according to data published by Russia's Defense Ministry and analyzed by ABC News.

Across August, the ministry said it shot down 18,174 Ukrainian drones -- at an average rate of around 586 each day -- as well as 56 Flamingo cruise missiles.

August was the fourth month in a row that the ministry reported a new record-high total for the number of Ukrainian drones shot down. In July, the ministry said it downed 13,312 Ukrainian drones, in June 11,914 craft and in May 9,418.

With a wary eye on Russia, Finland runs Europe's largest civil defense exercise since WWII
description: In a civil defense shelter hewn into rock, behind doors designed to withstand a nuclear or biological attack, two Finnish conscripts wearing hazmat suits and breathing masks are measuring radiation le...
fullText:
KUOPIO, Finland (AP) — In a civil defense shelter hewn into rock, behind doors designed to withstand a nuclear or biological attack, two Finnish conscripts wearing hazmat suits and breathing masks are measuring radiation levels as they take part in an exercise to turn a cave into a place of safety for thousands of people.

Inside, in what is normally a sports hall, hundreds of people are sleeping overnight on trestle beds.

More than 2,000 people including volunteers and students are taking part in the biggest civil defense exercise in Europe since the end of World War II. In the scenario, critical infrastructure in the central Finnish city of Kuopio, including power and water, has been disrupted by cyberattacks and there's the threat of missile strikes from Finland's neighbor, Russia.

The goal is for local authorities and ordinary people to rehearse what they would do if they came under attack for real.

But while underground bunkers and shelters may offer some protection from missiles, they are no defense against the campaign of sabotage and disruption that Western officials say Russia is carrying out across Europe. That has involved setting fires, attacking water facilities and power stations, and sending drones for sabotage into European Union airspace.

Finland's border with Russia stretches more than 830 miles (1,300 kilometers) from the Baltic Sea up to the Arctic Circle. In 2024, along with Sweden, Finland joined NATO, following Russian President Vladimir Putin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Until then, Finns were prepared to defend themselves against Russia largely alone.

Finland's defense, said retired Army Colonel Asko Muhonen, relies not only on the military but on the "mindset" of ordinary Finns who are ready to take responsibility for their country's security.

Muhonen, who organized the exercise in Kuopio, said that comes partly from the system of conscription which continued in Finland, even after the collapse of the Soviet Union.

Not everyone is happy about doing national service but "it's our duty to serve and protect this country like people have before us. That's why we have our independence," said Jyry Pietikainen, 23, a conscript who was taught how to run the Kuopio shelter overnight.

Finland also needs to learn lessons from Ukraine, Muhonen said.

While the biggest shelter in Kuopio can fit 7,000 people, Ukrainians sometimes only have a few minutes to run to a subway station or underground parking lot. That means people need a shelter they can reach easily that offers some form of protection — not necessarily one that can withstand a nuclear attack, he said.

Dmytro Untila, 20, a Ukrainian student at the university in Kuopio, was at home in Odesa when Russian missiles struck his city on Feb. 24, 2022, the first day of the war. He sheltered in the entrance hall of his building because he didn't have anywhere else to go, he said.

Training for such a situation would have definitely helped in Ukraine, he said, "because nobody knew this could happen."

The biggest threat to energy infrastructure in the Kuopio region is heavy snowfall, storms and bad weather, said Juha Räsänen, CEO at the Savon Voima electricity company.

But since the invasion of Ukraine, and the company's decision to stop buying Russian biofuel, the number of cyberattacks against the network has significantly increased, Räsänen said.

Last year, engineers also found at least 10 stickers placed on particularly vulnerable parts of the energy network infrastructure. Other energy companies in Finland have also found them and don't know where they came from, he said.

"If there was an explosion at that point, it could destroy a whole dam," Räsänen said. Drones have also been spotted over power lines but those responsible have not been identified, he said.

It is not possible to guard against all threats, Räsänen said, which is why it's important people are prepared to look after themselves without help for at least 72 hours — if the power supply goes out, or if water becomes undrinkable.

The Finnish Security and Intelligence Service said it investigated "a wide range of observations" and found nothing of concern.

Since 2022, people have been more vigilant because of the security situation and therefore have reported things like reflective stickers related to land survey works, it said in a statement. Drone sightings, it said, have "largely been explained by everyday occurrences."

"Small things are happening all the time," including Russian jamming of GPS signals, said Vuokko Lahtinen, 32, who was visiting a sauna in Kuopio.

For that reason, "the best defense of Finland is to make it not worth attacking," she said.

That relies on the country's military and defense forces but also Finnish people who feel like "we have something we want to fight for," she said.

In Finland, she said, there is a "general feeling of responsibility," which has grown out of local community groups and even initiatives such as recycling.

"On a very simple daily level, if you do things that matter, then it has a butterfly-wing effect," Lahtinen said.

In its wars with the Soviet Union, Finland lost around 11% of its territory, and more than 400,000 people, around 12% of the population, fled their homes from an area that is now in western Russia.

At Kuopio's veterans' museum, Risto Mönkkönen, 95, showed AP a piece of paper on which he had written down the dates the city was bombed and who died.

"I cannot forget it," he said explaining how, as a child, he and his father ran into a shelter just as a bomb hit, killing five of his father's friends.

Pirkko Naukkarinen, 102, recalled how, aged 16, she worked in a field kitchen by the front lines, sometimes sharing dugouts with soldiers and diving for cover in ditches as the Soviet air force attacked the retreating Finnish army.

Aili Toivanen, 92, told AP she was forced to leave her home twice over the various wars. Both times, her family was told by Finnish soldiers that they had one hour to pack their belongings.

The first time, she looked back and saw her home burning — set on fire by Finnish soldiers who did not want to leave anything behind, she said. The second time, she said, the Soviet air force bombed the family's departing train and they jumped out, hiding in ditches before they took refuge in Kuopio.

When Putin invaded Ukraine in 2022, she said, with tears in her eyes, that she worried she would have to leave her home for a third time.

At the shelter in Kuopio, thousands of people filed in, including schoolchildren and university students.

"Kids would need to know this, because they might have to do something alone. The adults can't always help," said Amanda Hill, 11, whose school studied in the shelter for the day.

Sitting on the floor of the shelter with his fellow conscripts, Pietikainen explained why it's not crazy to practice what happens in a crisis.

"We're Finns, so we're kind of pessimistic about life in a way," but history shows what can happen with Russia, he said.

When it comes to the threats from Moscow, Muhonen said, "don't believe what they say but observe what they do."

title: International equestrian body lifts ban on Russia
description: The International Equestrian Federation lifts its ban on Russian athletes and officials after four and a half years.
fullText:
The International Equestrian Federation has lifted its ban on Russian athletes and officials after four and a half years.

Riders, horses and officials from Russia and Belarus have been prohibited from representing their countries under their national flags at FEI events since March 2022, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

The international governing body will also allow events to be held in Russia as part of regulations that will come into effect on 5 October.

The move means participants from Russia and Belarus will no longer be required to compete as Neutral Individual Athletes.

The FEI's decision comes after the International Olympic Committee (IOC) announced in June that it would provisionally lift its suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee.

It means athletes from the region could potentially be cleared to represent Russia at the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles.

Following its announcement, the FEI said it would like to "take this opportunity to reiterate its support for the people of Ukraine".

title: All 16 of Russia's latest satellites for its Starlink rival failed to reach their intended orbit
description: The 16 satellites form the second batch of the Rassvet-3 constellation, which now only has 12 out of 32 launched satellites set for long-term orbit.
fullText:
After being cut off from Starlink, Russia is pushing to build its own version of the service.

But publicly available data shows its latest batch of 16 satellites hasn't reached operational orbit.

That's out of a total of 32 satellites launched so far, for a 37.5% success rate for now.

An entire batch of Russian low Earth orbit satellites, intended to help create Moscow's version of Starlink, has failed to reach or remain at their anticipated altitudes just over a month after launch.

The 16 Rassvet-3 satellites, launched on July 19, were originally supposed to orbit the Earth at an altitude of roughly 500 miles, according to the company developing the constellation, Bureau 1440.

But publicly available US Space Force data shows that, as of Tuesday, the Rassvet-3 satellites are instead orbiting at altitudes of between 190 miles and 250 miles.

Atmospheric drag at that altitude significantly shortens a satellite's operational lifespan. Without intervention, those conditions gradually pull satellites lower to Earth until they reenter the atmosphere and burn up or break apart.

Losing these 16 satellites — Bureau 1440's second batch of the Rassvet-3 — would be a significant setback for Moscow's ambition to create its own alternative to Starlink, a priority for the Kremlin after SpaceX cut off satellite internet service to Russian forces on February 1.

Rassvet-3 is meant to help fill that gap, but Bureau 1440 has launched only 32 satellites so far, including this latest batch.

Issues with the second satellite batch were first highlighted by journalist Anatoly Zak, who runs the website RussianSpaceWeb and identified two Rassvet-3 satellites in early August that were already headed for re-entry into Earth's atmosphere.

It's unclear what prevented the satellites from reaching higher altitudes. Positional data indicates that many of them engaged in maneuvers to climb upward, though none of these appear to have come close to helping the satellites reach their operational orbit yet.

"The apparent failure of all 16 satellites from the second launch to reach their intended operational altitudes suggests Russia may have been unprepared to accelerate constellation deployment at this pace and will likely face additional delays," wrote analysts from the Institute for the Study of War, a US-based think tank, on Monday.

Press services for Bureau 1440 and Roscosmos, Russia's space agency, did not immediately respond to comment requests sent outside regular business hours by Business Insider.

Bureau 1440 has said that it is planning "dozens of launches and hundreds of satellites" to form its total constellation.

Its first batch of 16, launched on March 23, saw 12 satellites reach and maintain altitudes of about 340 miles. That's still shy of the original 500-mile altitude that Russia initially set, and could indicate that Bureau 1440 shifted the target orbit closer to Earth.

Ukrainian estimates say the Kremlin will need roughly 200 to 250 operational satellites to maintain a stable internet network that Russian forces can use to communicate or operate combat drones.

SpaceX, by comparison, runs over 11,000 operational Starlink satellites.

A major bottleneck for the Rassvet-3 constellation is how they're launched. Russian spacecraft rely on the Soyuz-2.1b rocket, which has been used for 104 launches in the last two decades.

With 16 satellites per launch, keeping to that pace would mean Russia could launch roughly 80 Rassvet-3 satellites each year, taking more than two years to reach a constellation of at least 200.

And that assumes all the launched satellites remain operational in the long term.

With only 12 of the last 32 Rassvet-3 satellites reaching their apparent long-term orbits, the program has achieved a 37.5% success rate so far. SpaceX, by comparison, reported just 43 early mission failures or terminations among its first 1,383 production Starlink satellites, or a failure rate of about 3%.

Ukraine has also been attempting to undermine Russia's efforts. In mid-August, it said one of its FP-5 Flamingo long-range missiles struck a space center in Western Russia that produces the Soyuz rocket.

Satellite internet has become one of the most crucial communications tools of the war in Ukraine, with troops from both sides using the service to stay in contact with each other, direct drones, and update commanders.

Most prominently, Russia was previously found to be using Starlink terminals to relay signals to its attack drones, allowing them to bypass typical jamming measures and receive instructions at extended range.

title: Turkey's relations with Russia, China don't mean turning its back on the West, Erdogan says
description: Turkey is not backing away from the West as it seeks deeper ties with the East, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Wednesday as he headed back from a Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit....
fullText:
ISTANBUL (AP) — Turkey is not backing away from the West as it seeks deeper ties with the East, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Wednesday as he headed back from a Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit.

The conference in Kyrgyzstan saw Erdogan hold a one-on-one meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin at which they discussed further nuclear cooperation.

In comments made to journalists aboard the presidential plane, Erdogan reiterated Turkey's goal of becoming a full member of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, or SCO, whose ten current members include Russia, China, India and Iran.

"I would also like to particularly emphasize that Turkey's membership perspective in the organization does not mean a break from a bloc or turning our backs on the West," the president said.

Turning to the war in Ukraine, during which Ankara has maintained friendly relations with both Moscow and Kyiv, Erdogan said it was his and Putin's "expectation … that the war between Russia and Ukraine ends peacefully as soon as possible."

He also underlined the importance of maritime security in the Black Sea, where civilian shipping has come under increasing attack.

"There is a need for a mechanism that will permanently ensure the safety of commercial maritime transport in the Black Sea," Erdogan said, adding that it would be "beneficial" to prevent a "resurgence of the grain crisis."

Turkey brokered a grain deal in 2022 that opened Ukrainian ports and allowed the movement of Russian food and fertilizer. The agreement, which Putin pulled out of a year later, was vital for global food supplies, especially in Africa, the Middle East and Asia.

The SCO, founded in 2001, also includes Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Pakistan and Belarus. The growing bloc has been billed as a counterweight to U.S. global influence, although its goals and programs remain vague.

title: EU to hit back at Russia after drone attack as Germany probes new sabotage cases
description: BRUSSELS/BERLIN, Sept 2 (Reuters) - European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen vowed on Wednesday to increase pressure on Russia, including with new sanctions, after an attempted drone attack at L...
fullText:
BRUSSELS/BERLIN, Sept 2 (Reuters) - European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen vowed on Wednesday to increase pressure on Russia, including with new sanctions, after an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany that she said showed Moscow's growing "recklessness".

Airport workers last month found a drone ‌laden with explosives and a detonator at the airport, an important civilian freight and NATO logistics hub in eastern Germany that is also a base for ‌several giant Ukrainian Antonov An-124 cargo planes.

Germany blamed Moscow for the attack, characterising it as part of hybrid warfare meant to intimidate and cause divisions in countries that have rallied around Ukraine since Russia's 2022 invasion.

Russia denies ​involvement. It says it will respond to what its foreign ministry spokesperson called "anti-Russian action", and summoned Germany's top diplomat in Moscow.

"Europe and NATO will not just maintain our pressure on Russia; we will increase it, and we will not stop - not until Russia stops bombing and killing innocent children, men and women in Ukraine," von der Leyen said in Brussels after a meeting with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.

"Europeans are faced with the hard truth that this is the new normal. We have to step up, and that means being ready to respond to Russia's ‌recklessness faster and better."

The full scope of new sanctions was not ⁠immediately clear.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc was working on sanctions related to Russia's military complex, and France's foreign minister called for action against Russia's so-called "shadow fleet" of ships accused of circumventing energy sanctions.

Rutte said more drones and missiles had crossed into NATO airspace ⁠on Europe's eastern flank, and there was an increase in malign activities including the Leipzig attack.

"If Russia thinks we will be divided by the threat, or if they think we will be deterred from supporting Ukraine, they are mistaken," he said.

The EU and several EU member states summoned Russian embassy officials. Germany said it would close Russia's consulate general in Bonn and terminate its agreement with ​the ​Russian House cultural centre in Berlin.

TWO SUSPECTS IDENTIFIED, MEDIA OUTLETS SAY

Details of two Leipzig attack suspects were ​reported by German media outlets Sueddeutsche Zeitung, NDR and WDR.

Investigators have identified ‌the logistics coordinator and instructor behind the attack, the outlets reported.

The man, Russian-born but holding a Latvian passport, was believed to have ties to Russian intelligence, they said. He is thought to have flown into Berlin in late July and driven a rental car towards Leipzig. Two days before the failed drone attack, the suspect left Germany by plane, they reported.

The second suspect was a man from Belarus who also holds a Russian passport and is thought to have entered the country on an Italian tourist visa obtained in Minsk, the outlets said.

Germany's Public Prosecutor General did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Russia also did not immediately comment further on the case.

As the EU prepared ‌its response, Germany was grappling with two new suspected sabotage cases within 24 hours.

In the first, authorities ​were investigating vandalism at a substation in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia (NRW) that prompted lignite power plant units ​with 4,200 megawatts (MW) in combined capacity to go off the grid.

In the other, ​also on Tuesday, devices carrying conductive material damaged power lines at one of the most critical high-voltage nodes in the eastern state of Brandenburg.

NRW's interior ‌minister said the work of foreign powers or left-wing extremists could ​not be ruled out.

Brandenburg's interior minister, Jan Redmann, ​said there appeared to be parallels between the attacks but that investigations were at an early stage.

The incidents come at a sensitive time as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which calls for closer ties to Moscow, is topping polls before a state election this weekend.

Lawmaker Alexander Throm, an interior policy expert from Germany's ruling conservatives, ​said it was striking that such incidents were occurring before ‌elections.

"The clear goal is to unsettle the public. Of course, that is a goal shared not only by Russia but also by others, such as left-wing ​extremists," Throm told Reuters.

(Additional reporting by Bart H. Meijer, Padraic Halpin, Conor Humphries, John Irish, Dominique Vidalon, Charlotte Van Campenhout, Lili Bayer, Christoph Steitz, Matthias ​Inverardi and Miranda Murray; Writing by Matthias Williams; Editing by Sudip Kar-Gupta and Timothy Heritage)

title: FIA wrong to lift Russia ban - Ukraine minister
description: The FIA was wrong to lift the ban on Russian competitors because nothing has changed since it was imposed, the Ukrainian Minister for Youth and Sport says.
fullText:
Motorsport's governing body the FIA was wrong to lift the ban on Russian competitors because nothing has changed since it was imposed, the Ukrainian Minister for Youth and Sport says.

Matvii Bidnyi said: "The reasons why Russia was banned from international sports competition have not disappeared. Nothing changes and it became even worse."

Bidnyi said that the central rail station in the Ukrainian capital Kyiv had been bombed by a Russian drone on Wednesday just an hour before he spoke to BBC Sport.

"The air alert was just turning off," Bidnyi said. "Our kids, we all came from the bomb shelter. These attacks continue almost every day.

"Russia continues full-scale aggression against Ukraine. Belarus can continue to provide military support to Russia. Ukrainian people are still being killed every day. And Russian attacks become more and more brutal.

"I don't understand, and Ukrainian people, and I know that all European people don't understand what's happened, why now we must to make this policy softer."

Russian Athletics files new claim against sanctions

Russia could compete at LA 2028 Olympics

The ban on Russian and Belarussian competitors taking part in international motorsport events was imposed in February 2022, after Vladimir Putin ordered the invasion of Ukraine.

It was lifted on 3 August this year in a decision by the FIA's world motorsport council. This followed the International Olympic Association, with which the FIA is affiliated, lifting its own ban.

Bidnyi pointed out that other sports organisations had not followed this route, including World Athletics.

"When any federation lifts the ban and makes steps towards the aggressor, the terrorist state, it's always really, really sad," he said.

"It's a massive disappointment for everyone in Ukraine. And we think it undermines the collective pressure that the international community has been building against the aggressor.

"Unfortunately, there are a lot of international sports organisations trying to lift bans to release pressure from the aggressor. We can observe it in such a federation as judo, weightlifting, and then a lot of others.

"But we have strong partners and strong principle international organisations - for example, biathlon or athletics - who understand the responsibility of the international sports community for international order and justice."

The Russian Athletics Federation has filed a claim with the Court of Arbitration for Sport to challenge the sanctions imposed by World Athletics.

Bidnyi said: "In Russia, elite sport is deeply connected with the military and state propaganda system. It's one of the biggest whitewashing mechanisms. This is why we call it sportswashing."

The Ukraine government says that the war "has had a devastating impact on Ukrainian sport as a whole - since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion: 775 Ukrainian athletes and coaches have been killed by Russia", including three competitors in the Ukrainian Automobile Federation.

It says Russia "has made sport facilities their targets to continue killing - more than 925 sports facilities have been destroyed".

The FIA was contacted for comment. Last week, it issued a statement regarding the decision to lift the ban on Russian competitors.

A spokesperson said: "The FIA has updated the requirements for Russian and Belarusian drivers, national teams, competitors and officials following a vote by the world motorsport council. This follows an announcement by the IOC on 7th July and similar updates issued by other international sporting federations.

title: Russia economy could go ‘beserk’ with military-industrial complex, Putin envoy warns
description: Russia has hiked taxes, embarked on property redistribution, welcomed contributions from businesses to finance the war, and, most recently, threatened business owners who are not doing enough to protect their facilities from Ukrainian drones.
fullText:
MOSCOW (Reuters) - The Russian economy runs a risk of going "berserk" if it is run to focus entirely on the needs of the military-industrial complex, President Vladimir Putin's international development envoy was quoted as saying on Tuesday.

The comments by Boris Titov to business news outlet RBC were a rare sign of concern in Kremlin circles about the increasing pressure on the slowing economy to secure a victory in the 4-1/2-year war in Ukraine.

Titov, appointed in 2024 as Putin's special representative to international organizations for achieving sustainable development goals, is a wealthy businessman who used to own Russia's leading producer of sparkling wine. He led an influential business lobby and ran for president in 2018.

"Military and civilian economies have always existed in symbiosis everywhere. Many technical inventions that are useful for all originated within the military-industrial complex. The key lies in maintaining balance," Titov told RBC.

Russia has hiked taxes, embarked on property redistribution, welcomed contributions from businesses to finance the war, and, most recently, threatened business owners who are not doing enough to protect their facilities from Ukrainian drones.

War hawks and some government officials often refer to the reorganisation of the Soviet economy under dictator Josef Stalin during World War Two as a model, citing the wartime slogan "Everything for the front, everything for victory".

This approach is met with cautious but growing resistance from various sectors.

"This is not an economy at all, it's a kind of 'berserk mode' that can only exist for a very limited time, and the necessity of which should be considered very carefully," Titov said on the eve of a major economic forum that Putin will attend this week in Russia's Far East.

RBC, which conducted the interview, noted that the term berserk derived from mythological Norse warriors who entered a trance-like state, possibly drug-induced, that enabled them to fight ferociously and ignore pain.

The Russian economy is expected to grow at only 0.4% this year, and many non-military sectors are stagnating or shrinking. Ukrainian attacks on economic targets such as refineries, online retailers and oil and grain export infrastructure may push this growth rate even lower.

Titov's comments echo a statement by Moscow's technocrat mayor Sergei Sobyanin, who argued last month that "killing a normal economy is equivalent to killing the whole country".

fullText:
MOSCOW, Sept 1 (Reuters) - President Vladimir Putin said on Tuesday that Russia was winning the war in Ukraine and portrayed the Ukrainian leadership as "terrorists" with whom Moscow could not negotiate.

Putin, in his most detailed ‌comments on the war for many weeks, acknowledged that Ukrainian attacks inside Russia had inflicted real damage and said that drones ‌posed a particular challenge.

But he said that Russia was advancing on the battlefield and told reporters: "I have no doubt the enemy will crumble."

He declined to say when that ​would happen.

Rumours that Russia would be forced to order a new military mobilisation were "utter nonsense," he said.

PUTIN SAYS RUSSIAN ADVANCES ARE ACCELERATING

Four and a half years into the war, Russia controls about a fifth of Ukraine. U.S.-mediated peace talks broke off in February after the United States and Israel went to war with Iran.

Opinion polls suggest growing war fatigue in Russia and influential voices are warning about the strain on its economy.

But Putin struck ‌a confident, hawkish tone as he rattled through ⁠a detailed version of developments on the front line, saying Russian advances were accelerating.

Russian troops had captured 270 square km (104 sq miles) of the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine in August and two large groups of Ukrainian ⁠troops - one comprising 4,500 to 4,800 men, the other up to 2,000 - were surrounded, he said. Reuters could not independently verify those assertions.

Russia continues to advance towards the cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, Putin said, adding that Moscow's forces were preparing to launch massive strikes against energy infrastructure in Ukraine.

Putin said ​that ​Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy's warning to airlines that Ukrainian drones would effectively shut ​down Russian airspace sounded like "state terrorism" and that Moscow ‌would find a way to respond if it happened.

Speaking at a news conference after a summit in Kyrgyzstan, Putin said it was not possible to negotiate with "terrorists".

He also said, however, that Moscow was open to talks aimed at ending, rather than freezing, the war, and restated its willingness to talk to U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys.

"If someone makes, or can make, a tangible contribution to this process, we are all in favour," Putin said.

"The only thing we would want to avoid is the process spinning its wheels pointlessly. However, if someone is capable of bringing ‌something positive to these negotiations - which, as we understand it, are currently somewhat ​frozen - then, generally speaking, we are not opposed."

Putin specifically acknowledged that Ukrainian drone strikes ​had caused damage to Russian oil refineries, although without referring ​to widespread fuel shortages that have resulted from those attacks.

But he said that the level of protection had ‌improved, and "we only have 10% of our refineries left to ​repair".

Putin responded scathingly to an accusation ​by the German government on Tuesday that Russia was to blame for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport last month.

He said the government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz was pointing the finger at Moscow to distract from domestic problems and falling approval ratings.

Putin ​accused Germany of planting evidence in order to ‌frame Russia for the drone attack, but he did not say what he was basing that accusation on.

title: Ukraine dissects Russia’s Zircon missile as Moscow leans on harder-to-intercept weapons
description: A Ukrainian official says Russia's growing use of harder-to-intercept missiles marks a dangerous new stage as Patriot interceptor stocks run low.
fullText:
Ukraine's military intelligence published a detailed breakdown of Russia's Zircon missile.

The assessment reveals its components, speed, manufacturers, and foreign-made parts.

Russia has leaned more on hard-to-intercept missiles as Ukraine has gotten better at stopping other threats.

Ukraine's main military intelligence agency published a breakdown of Russia's Zircon missile, a weapon Moscow has increasingly employed in its intensifying strikes.

Russia has been investing heavily in advancing its missile arsenal, upgrading systems and making them harder for air defenses to intercept. That reaction to Ukrainian air-defense wins now represents a major challenge as interceptors run low.

On Monday, Ukraine's GUR, the country's military intelligence agency, shared details on Russia's 3M22 Zircon missile, including its components and production.

It also provided details on the main manufacturer NPO Mashinostroyeniya, a Russian defense company that is part of the Tactical Missiles Corporation, and foreign parts used in the weapon, which included some made by US companies. The disclosure also named more than 70 companies and dozens of people involved in its production.

In its new assessment, the GUR referred to Zircon as a ballistic missile, a departure from Russia's description of it as a hypersonic cruise missile. New details published by Ukraine describe it as a two-stage ballistic missile featuring a solid-fuel booster and a solid-fuel sustainer for flight.

Cruise missiles and ballistic missiles differ in how they fly and reach their targets. Ballistic missiles typically climb on a ballistic trajectory before descending at high speed toward their targets, while cruise missiles are jet-propelled and fly lower within the atmosphere.

Ukraine's assessment challenges Russia's long-standing characterization of the weapon.

The GUR also assessed that the Zircon is slower than claimed, with a maximum speed of Mach 6.8. Russia claims that the missile can reach speeds of Mach 9.

Russia has previously touted the Zircon missile as one of its "invincible" hypersonic weapons. It first used the missile against Ukraine in February 2024. At that time, Ukraine estimated that Russia had around 40 stockpiled.

The arsenal has since grown, though estimates vary, and Russia has increasingly fired these missiles in strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, leaning harder on more advanced missiles as Ukraine has demonstrated it can intercept other Russian systems.

"Since we learned to shoot down more than 90% of cruise missiles and drones with gasoline piston engines, Russia has decided to rely on ballistics and jet drones," Yehor Cherniev, the deputy chairman of the Ukrainian parliament's national security, defense, and intelligence committee, told Business Insider.

Russia did not immediately respond to Business Insider's request for comment on Ukrainian assessments of its weapons and motives.

Cherniev said that Ukraine assesses that Russia has reduced production of Kinzhal missiles because of accuracy issues and instead focused on producing Iskander and Zircon missiles. Russian forces have ramped up ballistic missile attacks on Ukraine this year, including debuting a new upgraded variant of its Iskander series, the Iskander-1000, earlier this summer.

These ballistic missiles are more difficult for Ukraine to intercept, and Russia's growing reliance on them comes as Ukraine struggles with shortages of critical air-defense interceptors. Ukraine relies on the US-made MIM-104 Patriot surface-to-air missile system to confront Russia's more difficult missiles, but it has warned that interceptor stocks are running low.

"This is a new and extremely dangerous stage of the war, which requires us to be more effective in the fight against high-speed jet drones, as well as additional assistance from the United States in the form of PAC-3 missiles for Patriot systems," Cherniev said.

MOSCOW, Aug 31 (Reuters) - Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi told Russian President Vladimir Putin on Monday that the war in Ukraine needed ‌to end for humanity's sake and that New Delhi would support ‌every peace effort to stop the fighting.

Modi, who made his comments at the start of ​talks with Putin in the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek, called Putin "my friend" and hailed growing economic ties between the two countries which he said were guided by the need to put the interests of both nations above all else.

India, along with ‌China, is one of ⁠the biggest buyers of Russian oil, which has helped Moscow replenish its budget since it sent tens of thousands of ⁠troops into Ukraine in 2022 and was hit with sweeping Western sanctions.

"As you are aware, India supports all peace efforts in this regard, and we shall continue ​to do ​so in the future," Modi told ​Putin on the sidelines of the ‌Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit, according to a Kremlin transcript of their exchange.

We need to move from endless war to an end to the ‌war, to a cessation of hostilities. And we ​will need to move precisely in this ​direction," said Modi who has ​said before that he wants a peace settlement for Ukraine.

title: Ukraine says its strikes on oil refineries have forced Russia to start importing jet fuel for its warplanes
description: Ukraine has been conducting a long-range strike campaign, hitting Russia's oil and gas facilities to try to hurt its economy and war effort.
fullText:
Ukraine said that its strikes on Russian oil facilities have pushed Moscow to import jet fuel.

Russia has a "shortage of domestic resources" as it tries to increase attacks and fly civilian jets.

Ukraine is attacking oil and gas facilities across Russia to try to hamper its fighting ability.

Ukraine said over the weekend that its strikes on Russian oil facilities have reduced production so much that Russia is now having to import fuel for its warplanes.

On Saturday, Ukraine's GUR, the country's military intelligence agency, said that "systematic and precise strikes by Ukraine's Defense Forces against Russia's oil-refining network have led to a significant reduction in jet fuel production in the Russian Federation."

It said that Russia's increasing air attacks against Ukraine, "combined with the need to sustain civilian air transport, have resulted in a shortage of domestic resources."

"To meet the needs of military and civilian aviation, Russia, which for decades has positioned itself as an energy superpower, has officially introduced a temporary ban on the export of its own aviation fuel and is being forced to seek ways to import foreign Jet A-1 aviation fuel," the GUR said.

That fuel is compatible with a range of Russian military aircraft used to launch missiles and bombs, as well as jet-powered drones. The GUR added that Russia is now fueling its Il-76MD-90A military transport with fuel outside manufacturer recommendations.

The GUR said that Russia had purchased at least 70,000 tonnes of aviation fuel from South Korea and Egypt that was delivered on three shadow fleet tankers. The fleet is a network of vessels that Russia uses to circumvent Western sanctions through hidden ownership, among other methods.

The GUR Saturday said that Russian efforts to "circumvent sanctions will inevitably receive an appropriate response."

Ukraine is conducting a major long-range strike campaign targeting oil and gas facilities inside Russia in a bid to damage the country's economy, which depends heavily on the energy sector, and frustrate its ability to continue its invasion of Ukraine. The strikes have hit targets hundreds of miles into Russia.

Ukraine refers to these strikes against Russia's economy as "long-range sanctions." Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy promised this month that "there will be more Ukrainian deep strikes, which should demonstrate to Russia and the Russians that peace is necessary."

Ukraine has significantly increased the pace of these strikes this year and claimed a host of wins against targets this month, including strikes on refineries, processing facilities, and terminals. The country has said that some sites have halted operations as a result.

Zelenskyy said in June that nearly 40% of Russia's primary oil refining capacity was offline as of the previous month. And he said this month that it remains a priority for Ukraine.

Russia's economy is heavily dependent on oil and gas. Western sanctions have affected the industry, but Russia also received a reprieve when the war in Iran limited other energy sources by closing the Strait of Hormuz, a route Russia does not rely on. Kyiv is trying to restore some of that pressure.

Ukraine has primarily used homemade cruise missiles and drones to hit targets inside Russia. Though Western partners provided long-range weapons, restrictions on their use inside Russia forced Ukraine's booming defense industry to develop domestic solutions.

Ukraine has unveiled new weaponry with longer ranges in recent months to deepen its campaign, including drones with ranges exceeding 1,800 miles.

Mykhailo Fedorov, Ukraine's former defense minister, said this month that Ukraine could be capable of hitting Russian territory with domestically made ballistic missiles within the next three to six months. These weapons typically have longer ranges and move much faster than cruise missiles.

Ukraine is fighting against barrages of Russian strikes on its territory that are stretching its air defenses thin. A key target Kyiv seeks to pursue is the missile launchers inside Russia.

Russia has been intensifying its strikes on Ukraine. Zelenskyy said on Sunday that in the last week, Russia launched almost 2,000 attack drones, more than 1,600 glide bombs, and 31 missiles, including North Korean ballistic missiles, at Ukraine.

Ukraine's long-range strike campaign, which is focused solely on legitimate military targets rather than cities and civilian infrastructure like Russian strikes, has yet to push Moscow toward negotiations for ending hostilities, but Kyiv hopes that the fuel shortages will raise the cost of the war and constrain some attacks.

fullText:
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russian forces relentlessly battered Kyiv and cities in the region around the Ukrainian capital for a fifth straight day Monday, leaving some supermarket shelves bare after repeated strikes on warehouses as Ukraine reels from attacks with jet-powered drones.

Russia has intensified its aerial attacks in recent months, more than four years after it invaded its neighbor. Almost constant air raid alerts in the Kyiv region in recent days have severely disrupted daily routines. Two major attacks in July killed almost 50 civilians, and a strike on Saturday killed at least 38 people.

Classes were due to resume at Ukrainian schools on Tuesday, but it was unclear whether parents would send their children. Schools have air raid shelters, and classes can also be held online. But about 1 million textbooks have been destroyed in Russian attacks on publishing houses, potentially delaying deliveries for the start of the school year, Ukraine's Education Ministry said earlier this month.

"Right now, Russia's tactic is to wear down Ukraine and Ukrainians — first and foremost, our people," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on social media late Sunday.

Ukraine has also tried to make Russian civilians feel the burden of war by hammering major online retailers and oil facilities. The attacks have brought shortages for ordinary Russians, though its strikes have not been as deadly for civilians.

A pall of black smoke drifted over Kyiv on Monday morning. In Brovary and Boryspil, cities in the Kyiv region, the aerial attacks struck several warehouses and four people were wounded, said Tymur Tkachenko, head of the regional military administration.

Zelenskyy conceded on social media that Ukraine is struggling to counter fast-flying jet-propelled drones that Russia is increasingly deploying.

Between Thursday and Sunday, Russia fired almost 1,500 drones at Ukraine, and around 800 of them were jet-powered, Zelenskyy said.

Combat aircraft are currently trying to stop the jet-powered versions while Ukraine looks to develop more effective technology.

"Four companies have developed the relevant interceptor drones, and one company has the most successful technology," Zelenskyy said. He didn't elaborate.

Repeated Russian strikes on food distribution centers and retail hubs have disrupted Ukrainian logistics, leaving some supermarket shelves bare and fueling public concern about shortages.

Those fears prompted Zelenskyy adviser Serhii Beskrestnov to say on social media Monday that Ukraine will not go hungry.

He urged the public not to give in to rumors, disinformation or panic, saying producers and retailers are currently restructuring supply chains.

He added that European countries would be ready to fill any food supply shortfall, if necessary.

At the same time, Russia has kept up its attacks on Ukraine's power grid, seeking to leave civilians cold and without running water in the approaching winter.

Russian forces launched what officials said was a massive overnight drone attack on Ukraine's northern Chernihiv region, which borders Russia, where an energy facility was damaged, according to Viacheslav Chaus, head of the regional military administration. He did not provide details of the damage.

The Russian Defense Ministry said Sunday it is preparing "massive strikes" on Ukraine's energy infrastructure.

Russia overnight shot down 239 Ukrainian drones over 14 Russian regions, occupied Crimea and the waters of the Black Sea, the Defense Ministry in Moscow said Monday.

A Ukrainian missile attack Sunday evening on the Russian border city of Belgorod killed three people, acting regional Gov. Alexander Shuvayev said.

Also, a Ukrainian drone attack wounded four people in the Russian city of Yekaterinburg, regional Gov. Denis Pasler said Monday. Yekaterinburg is Russia's fourth-biggest city, located over 2,000 kilometers (1,250 miles) from Ukraine's border, and is an industrial hub.

Hatton reported from Lisbon, Portugal. Elise Morton in London contributed to this story.

Follow the AP's coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

title: Leaders of China, Russia and India are among heads of state meeting to counter US influence
description: The leaders of China, Russia and India are among the heads of state gathering in Kyrgyzstan this week for the summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, a group billed as a counterweight to U.S....
fullText:
The leaders of China, Russia and India are among the heads of state gathering in Kyrgyzstan this week for the summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, a group billed as a counterweight to U.S. global influence.

Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi are attending the events in Bishkek, the capital of the Central Asian nation.

Multiple one-on-one meetings are scheduled on the sidelines of the summit, including one between Putin and Xi on Monday, as well as talks between the Russian leader and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Tuesday, the day of the official SCO sessions.

Russia, now 4½ years into its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and Iran, six months into a war with the United States and Israel, see the summit as an important platform to strengthen their relations with non-Western partners.

The SCO was founded in 2001 by China, Russia and four Central Asian states as a security forum. Over the past quarter-century, it has grown in size and influence, although its goals and programs remain vague and its brand recognition low.

It now includes 10 nations: Russia, China, India, Iran, Pakistan, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. Many other countries have the status of "dialogue partners."

Along with Russia, China has presented the SCO as an alternative to Western-aligned organizations like the G7, and in recent years has wanted to expand the scope and influence of the organization, pledging development and financial assistance.

China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said last week that the organization has successfully "explored a new path for regional cooperation." Beijing has consistently promoted the idea of an alternative world order with Russia's support.

For many SCO members, the summit will be an opportunity to show that they maintain strong ties on the global stage despite souring relations with the West.

The organization is not a unified political or military bloc, however, and analysts note that its members have significant disagreements and their own distinct interests.

For countries such as India, however, experts say the summit is likely to be more about optics and strategic signaling than substantive outcomes.

The forum is heavily influenced by China and includes Pakistan as a member — both of which are rivals for India.

Dinakar Peri, a fellow in security studies at Carnegie India, said the SCO gives India a seat at the table in a region increasingly shaped by competition among the larger powers, allowing it to protect its interests, track shifting geopolitical currents and project itself as a reliable stakeholder.

"While it may not entirely shape the agenda, it gives New Delhi a first-hand view of the region and allows it to hedge its position with others," Peri said.

Turkey, which holds partner status within the SCO, also seeks to use the platform to strengthen its position in the region.

It views SCO membership as part of a balanced foreign policy that seeks to maintain its traditional ties with the West as a part of NATO, while strengthening its influence in Eurasia.

President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who brought his country into the SCO as a "dialogue partner" in 2012, has repeatedly stated that he wants Turkey to become a permanent member. While Turkey has close trade ties with the European Union under a 1995 trade deal, its EU membership bid has stalled for more than 25 years.

Andrew Wilks in Istanbul, Turkey, Huizhong Wu in Bangkok, and Aijaz Hussain in New Delhi contributed.

title: Russia is slowly grinding through the Donbas as Ukraine braces for a brutal fight over its last strongholds
description: Russia is grinding deeper into the Donbas, where Ukrainian troops are preparing for a costly fight over the region's last major defensive bastions.
fullText:
Russia is advancing slowly through the Donbas as Ukraine prepares to defend its last major strongholds.

Ukrainian commanders say the fight for Kramatorsk and Sloviansk could become brutal battles of attrition.

Analysts warn the outcome may hinge on Ukraine's ability to keep troops supplied under relentless drone and air attacks.

There is a moment before the camera begins rolling when the young Ukrainian commander says, "History is repeating itself for us in the Donbas. Unfortunately." Then he falls silent.

A few minutes later, the man, known by the call sign "Fleshka," takes a seat on a weight bench in the garden of a house in an eastern Ukrainian village, just a 30-minute drive from the nearest Russian troops. Every morning, he benches 80 kilograms here before returning to the screens where he coordinates the destruction of Russian assault units through the live feeds from his drone operators.

"I hope it will be a long fight. This is our land, and we will fight for every meter of it," Fleshka says once the camera is rolling. A few meters away stands his comrade "Sascha," another unit commander with the 33rd Brigade. "It's going to be a brutal meat grinder," he predicts, describing a bloody war of attrition. "But I'm glad to be part of it."

Fleshka, 24, and Sascha, 26, belong to a new generation of young Ukrainian commanders helping lead the defense of the last Ukrainian-held bastions in the Donbas. Both have spent years fighting on the front lines. They were involved in the drawn-out Battle of Bakhmut in 2023 and later took part in Ukraine's offensive in Russia's Kursk region at the end of 2024. Today, each man is responsible for more than 80 soldiers serving in a combined drone-and-infantry unit.

The Donbas is comprised of the Luhansk and Donetsk regions. Russia has captured almost all of Luhansk, while Ukraine controls just under one-fifth of the Donetsk region, an area of roughly 5,000 square kilometers, about five times the size of Berlin.

The question is increasingly not whether Putin's army will seize the remaining Ukrainian-held territory in Donbas, but when.

According to information obtained by WELT from conversations with representatives of a leading European intelligence service, Russian forces could reach the outskirts of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk by early 2027. The two cities form the center of the last major Ukrainian defensive belt in the Donbas.

Intelligence officials predict that Russian troops could complete the conquest of most of the region by next year. The human cost of that campaign, however, would likely be staggering. Hundreds of thousands more Russian soldiers could be killed or seriously wounded in the process.

Since the start of the war in 2022, Russia's military has suffered around 1.4 million casualties, according to estimates by analysts at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, including up to 450,000 dead and nearly one million wounded.

Military analyst Franz-Stefan Gady, author of Attack: When War Comes to Us, offers a somewhat more optimistic assessment for Ukraine. Russia's advance, he argues, is progressing at its slowest pace since winter. "At the current rate, Donetsk region would not be fully captured until the early 2030s," he says.

A slowdown, however, should not be mistaken for a stabilization of the front lines. In some sectors, Kyiv's military position is deteriorating. Russia enjoys local superiority in first-person-view drones on certain stretches of the front, in some cases by a ratio of 10 to one. Meanwhile, 3,000-kilogram guided glide bombs continue to inflict heavy losses on Ukrainian forces in front-line areas.

Gady believes it's possible that Russian troops could reach Kramatorsk and Sloviansk as early as spring or summer 2027, but only under one condition.

"Russia needs mobilization if it wants to sustain or increase the current pace," he says. "Moscow is unlikely to do this before the elections, and if it does, Ukraine has no equivalent response available."

According to Gady, Russia's General Staff estimates that newly mobilized troops need around four months before they can have a meaningful impact at the front. A mobilization this autumn could therefore begin to shape events during the first half of 2027.

Col. Markus Reisner of the Austrian Armed Forces says Russia's summer offensive has so far fallen well short of Kremlin expectations. Nevertheless, Putin's troops continue to advance "slowly but steadily".

The decisive factor in the battle for the Donbas, he argues, will be Ukrainian logistics.

"The single most important capability influencing the fight for the Ukrainian defensive belt around Kramatorsk and Sloviansk is the ability to supply the defenders in those cities. If Russian forces succeed in disrupting those supply routes, Ukrainian defenders will be able to hold out only for a limited period."

Already, much of the resupply effort relies on heavy multicopter drones and uncrewed ground vehicles. Russian forces are systematically targeting these systems while simultaneously attempting to prevent the reinforcement and rotation of Ukrainian troops.

Reisner's warning is stark: "If the Ukrainians fail to break this vicious cycle, the defensive belt will fall." Ukrainian brigade commanders also acknowledge that Russia ultimately possesses the resources required to conquer the Donbas.

"Of course, Russia has the potential," Vadym Krykun, commander of the Lubart Brigade, told WELT earlier this year. "It remains the second-largest army in the world. The question is how far Russia is willing to go, how much further it is prepared to mobilize its economy and its population."

Krykun has been fighting in Donbas for more than a decade. Russian troops first entered the region in 2014, and fighting has continued ever since.

As recently as last year, there were hopes that a settlement over eastern Ukraine might pave the way for a ceasefire or even peace. At the end of 2025, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy proposed withdrawing Ukrainian troops from parts of the Donbas as part of a peace initiative, on the condition that Russia also withdraw and that the area be converted into an internationally monitored demilitarized zone, or "free economic zone." The Kremlin rejected the proposal, which was also supported by the United States.

The troops led by Fleshka and Sascha operate heavy "Vampire" and "Nemesis" bomber drones in the Donbas that can strike targets up to 50 kilometers away. They are complemented by reconnaissance drones, drone-based mine-laying systems, and ground robots.

"Our primary focus right now is eliminating their drone operators," Sascha says. "We located the enemy, bombed the position, and mined the area around it. So I would advise them to leave their foxholes and get as far away as possible."

His soldiers, he says, are doing everything they can to keep Ukrainian infantry alive. "The longer the infantry survives, the longer the cities hold."

Fleshka explains that the so-called "death zone," the area in which soldiers must expect drone attacks at any moment, has expanded dramatically in recent months.

The kill zone now stretches 20 kilometers deep in some places, and up to 50 kilometers in others.

"When they use small groups and start moving, and we detect them, nobody wants to let them get away," Sascha says. "Our priority is to eliminate them. There are so many Russians that they simply do not care. I don't know, it's a complicated subject. We eliminate them without much difficulty, but there are just so many of them."

Sascha then describes the Russian tactic in greater detail.

"The enemy sends people forward one at a time. Ten groups essentially means ten individuals."

If one reaches the designated position, another ten groups are sent forward. Eventually, one gets through, then another, then another, until six soldiers have assembled and can continue advancing together.

"Well, let's put it this way: it's a good tactic. An interesting tactic. I haven't come across anything quite like it before," he says.

According to Gady, this method of gradual infiltration and attrition is central to Russia's approach. "Cities do not fall through breakthroughs or house-to-house combat. They fall through exhaustion."

Fleshka fears that Druzhkivka could be the next city to come under serious threat.

"They have shifted their focus toward Sloviansk. They are already fighting in Mykolaivka."

Sascha also expects a fierce battle for Sloviansk. He insists that his men are ready. "It will be like Chasiv Yar. But how long did they assault Chasiv Yar? About a year, if I remember correctly."

He points to the terrain surrounding Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. "The landscape here works in our favor and against theirs. We hold the high ground and have cover. It will be a brutal meat grinder."

Experts doubt that a complete Russian conquest of the Donbas would necessarily persuade the Kremlin to enter serious ceasefire negotiations. "Putin will adjust his war aims depending on the condition of Ukraine's defenders," says Reisner.

Russia is presently targeting what he describes as one of Ukraine's Achilles heels: the critical shortage of air-defense ammunition, particularly for Patriot systems.

"The first major attacks indicate that Putin plans to subject Ukraine to sustained large-scale strikes this winter. He is following a strategy of exhaustion inspired by Svechin, the well-known Soviet military theorist."

Gady argues that, from Moscow's perspective, the Donbas may represent only an intermediate objective.

"The Donbas is an interim goal, not the final one. Russia's strategic objective remains bringing Ukraine back into its sphere of influence. According to Ukrainian intelligence, planning already exists for future operations toward Mykolaiv, Kherson, and Odesa, even if no timelines have been defined."

A genuine de-escalation, he adds, is politically difficult for Moscow.

"It would require scaling back Russia's war economy and explaining to the population why the war is being brought to an end."

title: Ukraine defence chief to outline war plan as Kyiv seeks more funds
description: Ukraine's new defence minister said he would outline a "clear vision" for Kyiv's partners of how his country plans to fight Russia, as the government tries ‌to bring forward p...
fullText:
KYIV, Aug 30 (Reuters) - Ukraine's new defence minister said he would outline a "clear vision" for Kyiv's partners of how his country plans to fight Russia, as the government tries ‌to bring forward part of a European Union loan to help cover a $27 billion military budget ‌deficit.

Ukraine relies heavily on foreign funds to continue its war effort, now in its fifth year, with the EU committing €90 billion in ​financing through 2027.

In comments to reporters released on Sunday, Yevhenii Khmara said Kyiv would seek to bring forward part of the €45 billion loan planned for next year, as well as lobby allies for greater contributions and new countries that had not yet given.

"Ukraine will present partners with a clear vision and a clear plan: what tasks the Defence ‌Forces face, what projects are needed ⁠for this, what results must be achieved, and within what timeframes," he said.

The EU has earmarked €45 billion each for 2026 and 2027, allowing Ukraine to channel record funds toward ⁠defence. President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said last week that Kyiv had spent more than expected in the first half of the year.

Khmara took over as defence minister last month from Mykhailo Fedorov, whose dismissal sparked rare wartime ​protests that ​prompted Zelenskiy to also fire his unpopular military chief.

A ​former special-forces commander who led Ukraine's deep-strike campaign ‌against Russia, Khmara said he shared a "common vision" with new top general Mykhailo Drapatyi. He pledged to be receptive to front-line troops and commanders.

"It is the soldiers on the ground who best see what needs to change," he said.

Kyiv is seeking to seize the initiative from Moscow, partly by stepping up long-range drone strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, defence manufacturing and logistics.

But it faces a critical shortage of manpower and air defences to ‌fend off Russian air attacks on Ukrainian cities. Kyiv's military has ​also faced controversy over abuses and mismanagement in recruitment and on ​the battlefield.

Khmara also said Ukraine needs "proper decisions" ​to preserve lives and a clear vision throughout the ranks for how to fight and ‌end the war.

"This vision must be communicated ​down the chain to commanders ​and units carrying out missions at the front every day," he said.

Khmara said Ukraine has tested four potential interceptors to shoot down the jet-powered drones Russia is increasingly firing at Ukraine. The goal, he ​added, is to eventually be able ‌to produce thousands of units.

Swarms of the high-speed drones have plagued the capital Kyiv for ​four consecutive days, killing residents, damaging homes and warehouses and upending daily life.
